entry.hook: 如意金箍棒 / As-You-Will Golden-Banded Rod (As-You-Will Golden-Banded Rod) — It is not a weapon forged for war, but a cosmological pillar forged to anchor the ocean's pulse. Its true name is not a promise of victory, but a sentence of eternal labor: a one-hundred-thirty-thousand-five-hundred-pound iron rod that bends to the will of a single master, while the earth beneath the Eastern Sea slowly breaks apart in its shadow.

body.body_1:
如意金箍棒 / As-You-Will Golden-Banded Rod  
定海神珍铁 / Orihalcon Tidal-Calming Pillar  
Artifact Tier: Fa Bao (法宝)  
Current Holder: Sun Wukong (孙悟空)  
Current Status: In active service, kept within the ear cavity of its master as a form of portable containment; the Eastern Sea dragon vein continues to suffer accumulated damage from every activation of its tide-calming runes.
body.body_2: The As-You-Will Golden-Banded Rod is classified as a Fa Bao (法宝), a refined treasure sealed with immense spiritual energy and lawful essence. Its core capability is the manifestation of the "As-You-Will" principle—an internalized law that allows the rod to change its size, length, and weight at the holder's command. The rod's mass rests at a fixed baseline of exactly thirteen thousand five hundred jin (approx. 8,100 kg in modern terms under a 0.6 kg-per-jin standard, though the precise mythic weight varies across textual traditions). It exerts a natural suppression effect over water currents, dragon veins, and all aquatic spiritual forces, having once been planted into the Eastern Sea's abyssal eye to stabilize the ocean's pulse. When its runes are activated in combat, the rod generates resonant lightning strikes that can shatter mountains and split the earth. No precise upper limit to its expansion or mass multiplication is recorded in stable mythic tradition; the tradition treats its upper reach as a matter of the holder's cultivation depth and not a fixed ceiling. The minimum requirement for wielding the rod is a physical constitution capable of bearing its baseline mass—any lesser being who attempts to lift it without the rod's recognition faces immediate crushing internal injury.
body.body_3: The rod's core material is Nine-Turn Smelted Fine Iron (九转镔铁), a substance refined in the crucible of Lord Lao Zi's (太上老君) Tushita Palace (兜率宫). The iron was subjected to repeated cycles of smelting through Samadhi True Fire (三昧真火), a Strange Fire (异火) capable of melting not only metal but the structural laws binding matter together. The refinement process consumed vast quantities of celestial spirit stones and primal energy from the palace's reserves; the tradition records that the Samadhi True Fire dimmed for a hundred years after this expenditure. The rod was originally commissioned by Yu the Great (大禹), the mythic sage-king of flood control, who required a divine pillar capable of measuring the depths of rivers and seas. After the flood-taming campaign concluded, the rod was cast into the Eastern Sea as the Tidal-Calming Pillar (定海神珍铁). It was driven into the abyssal eye, extracting the entire water-vein stabilizing law of that sea and permanently anchoring it within the rod's matrix. This extraction caused the Eastern Sea's abyssal eye to become a wound that requires the constant infusion of true essence from the dragon clan of that sea to prevent collapse. The material itself—the Nine-Turn Smelted Iron—retains no independent consciousness but carries the residual imprint of the forcibly extracted tidal law, which expresses itself as an unending gravitational pull toward the sea's original axis of stability.
body.body_4: The rod does not possess a Qi Ling (器灵) in the conventional sense of a sealed soul. No living being was sacrificed and imprisoned within its structure. Its power and responsiveness derive instead from two sources: first, the residual lawful imprint of the tidal-suppression principle extracted from the Eastern Sea's abyssal eye; second, an iron core infused with the "As-You-Will" property through Lord Lao Zi's forging, which gives the rod a native capacity to bend its physical form to a recognized wielder's command. The tradition describes this responsiveness as a form of resonance rather than conversation. The rod does not speak, think, or develop independent desire. It does, however, carry a deep structural memory of its original function as the Tidal-Calming Pillar, which manifests as a latent hostility toward uncontrolled water forces and an instinctive suppression of dragon veins. This is not the hatred of an imprisoned spirit but the persistent orientation of a material permanently shaped by a cosmic law.
body.body_5: The binding between the rod and its recognized wielder, Sun Wukong, follows a specific ritual logic rather than a contract of mutual feeding. When Wukong first entered the Eastern Sea's palace and approached the pillar, the rod recognized him as its destined master through a combination of innate affinity and physical capacity. It then transformed itself into a size suitable for use and accepted his grip. This is classified as a form of Ren Zhu (认主) but not of the blood-sacrifice type. No intentional offering of blood, soul access, or life-essence payment occurred. The rod's condition for recognition appears to be sufficient cultivation depth and physical constitution to bear its baseline mass, combined with an undefined quality of spiritual compatibility. The relationship is not symbiotic in the sense of mutual consumption—the rod does not drain the holder's vitality during normal use. However, if a wielder of insufficient cultivation attempts to lift it or command it through forced will, the rod's residual lawful imprint reacts as an opposing force, crushing the intruder's meridians by reflecting their own exerted power back into their body. This is not an act of malice but a mechanical consequence of the rod's lawful inertia resisting inferior cultivation. Several dragon princes of the Eastern Sea are recorded in textual tradition as having attempted to lift the rod, only to have their bones and meridians shattered by the rod's passive resistance. No known instance of Shi Zhu (噬主)—the artifact devouring its recognized master—exists in the rod's stable textual record.
body.body_6:
The rod's recorded history of wielders is brief and dominated by a single stable figure. The tradition recognizes only one fully recognized master:
- **Yu the Great (大禹)** — The mythic sage-king of the flood-quelling era. Yu used the rod as the Tidal-Calming Pillar, a tool for measuring the depths of rivers and seas and stabilizing turbulent water currents. His relationship with the rod was functional rather than martial; he did not wield it as a weapon but planted it into the earth as a surveying instrument and law-anchoring device. After the flood campaign concluded, Yu left the rod in the Eastern Sea, where it became the abyssal anchor. Yu's own fate is not recorded in direct relation to the rod; he is believed to have passed into the celestial bureaucracy as one of the Five Emperors, with no record of harm from the rod.
- **Sun Wukong (孙悟空)** — The Monkey King, born of primal stone on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. Wukong claimed the rod from the Eastern Sea dragon palace in a famous episode of his career. He has wielded it continuously ever since, through his rebellion against Heaven, his imprisonment under the Buddha's hand, and his subsequent service as the protector of the monk Tang Sanzang on the Journey to the West. Wukong has not been devoured or significantly harmed by the rod. The rod has, however, been temporarily taken from him during his imprisonment, during which it remained inert, awaiting his return. No other individual is recorded in the stable mythic tradition as having successfully wielded the rod. Local variant traditions and later literary expansions sometimes add other attempted handlers, but these are not treated as canon within the mainstream textual record.
body.body_7:
The rod's most famous and fully documented activation occurred during Sun Wukong's rebellion against Heaven, recorded in the Journey to the West and earlier Ming-dynasty novels. When Wukong faced the celestial army, the rod's combat profile was fully demonstrated:
- It expanded to a length and thickness that allowed Wukong to sweep through entire battalions of heavenly soldiers in a single stroke.
- Its rune-engraved surface discharged lightning with each swing, creating shockwaves that toppled celestial gates and shattered defensive formations.
- When Wukong struck the ground with it, the rod's tidal-suppression law interacted with the earth's own dragon veins, causing localized seismic collapse.

The most significant recorded activation in terms of lawful intervention was Wukong's face-off against the Four Heavenly Kings and Erlang Shen (二郎神). During this battle, the rod was used at full combat extension for an extended period, with the tidal-calming law actively suppressing the water-based divine abilities of the celestial army's aquatic generals.

No upper-limit threshold or time limitation on the rod's use is given in the stable textual tradition. The rod's power is presented as functionally boundless while its law-holding integrity remains intact. However, the tradition does record a non-combat limitation: each activation of the rod's tidal-calming runes generates a measurable shockwave through the dragon veins of the Eastern Sea, causing incremental structural damage. The accumulated damage has, over the centuries of Wukong's active use, resulted in partial collapses of certain deep-sea trenches within the Eastern Sea's abyssal ecosystem. No record exists of the rod ever self-destructing or undergoing Qi Ling (器灵) rampage due to overuse.
body.body_8: No paired or complementary artifact is recorded in the stable mythic tradition as being directly linked to the rod through a design pair or mutual resonance. The rod's closest analog in function and origin is the Nine-Plate Divine Staff of the Dragon Kings, but no reciprocal binding is indicated. No specific counter-artifact is known to naturally suppress the rod's power. The rod was originally forged from Nine-Turn Smelted Iron within Lord Lao Zi's Tushita Palace crucible, but it was not created as a fragment of any higher primordial armament. Its material origin is independent: the iron was smelted from celestial deposits rather than salvaged from the broken remains of a Tai Gu Shen Bing (太古神兵). The rod shares a circumstantial connection with the Flood-Taming Pearls of the dragon clan, but this is a thematic resonance rather than a lawful relationship.
body.body_9: The rod is currently in the possession of Sun Wukong, who keeps it stored within his ear cavity as a personal holding method. Its physical status is fully intact; no damage or degradation has been recorded. It remains in a state of active responsiveness, capable of being summoned instantly through Wukong's will. While Wukong's master is alive and active, the rod remains in service. If Wukong were to perish or become permanently incapacitated, the rod would likely return to a dormant state, awaiting the next holder who meets its recognition criteria. No tradition describes an active search for a new master while Wukong lives.
body.body_10: The rod's primary pool of access in the mythic record are the Ming-dynasty novel Journey to the West and the earlier San Sui Ping Yao Zhuan (三遂平妖传). No physical artifact, surviving inscription, or monument is known to correspond to the rod in the material world. The Dragon Palace of the Eastern Sea is described in literary tradition as the rod's former resting place, but this is a mythologized location rather than a confirmed physical site.
body.body_11: The rod's existence is deeply interwoven with multiple figures across the mythic record. Its original commissioner, Yu the Great, represents the earliest layer of the rod's biography, where it served as a surveying instrument and law-anchoring device during the primordial flood-quelling era. After Yu departed for the celestial realm, the rod remained in the Eastern Sea's abyssal eye as a permanent anchor for the ocean's pulse. In this dormant state, it was periodically encountered by members of the Eastern Sea Dragon Clan, who recognized its lawful inertia but could not match its recognition requirement. The rod's most famous and defining relationship is with Sun Wukong, the Monkey King born from primordial stone on Huaguo Mountain. Wukong's recognition by the rod is a foundational event in his mythic career, and the rod's subsequent role as his primary weapon spans the entirety of his story arc—from the kingdom of monkeys, through his celestial rebellion, imprisonment, and final redemption as the protector of the pilgrim Xuanzang on the Journey to the West. The rod's lawful suppression of water forces also places it in indirect tension with the Water Ape General and other aquatic enemies encountered during Wukong's pilgrimage, though no artifact-versus-artifact confrontation with these figures is recorded.

guide.guide_1: Imagine, if you will, a weapon that is not forged for killing but designed for a far stranger purpose: to hold an entire ocean still. The As-You-Will Golden-Banded Rod started its existence not as a club for beating demons into submission, but as a surveyor's stake—a one-hundred-thirty-thousand-five-hundred-pound iron pillar planted into the Eastern Sea's abyssal eye to stop the water from moving. It was a law-anchor. A calibration rod for the entire ocean's pulse. That original function never truly went away. Even now, every time Sun Wukong swings it, every time those runes along its surface glow and lightning crackles out, the rod is vibrating deep at a frequency that fractures the seafloor beneath the Eastern Sea. The rod is not just following the Monkey King's will. It is also remembering its original job: pressing down on something that should not rise. And the Eastern Sea, one shudder at a time, is paying the accumulated debt of that memory.
guide.guide_2: If you have seen any version of the Journey to the West—and I suspect you have, whether through the 1986 TV series, the animated movies, or the countless adaptations in video games and comics—you have seen this rod in action. Sun Wukong pulls a tiny needle from his ear. He mutters "Big, big, big," and suddenly he is holding a golden-banded iron pillar that can flatten mountain peaks. It is the most recognizable weapon in all of Chinese myth. But here is the thing about those adaptations: they almost never show you what happens *underneath*. The rod's true name is the Tidal-Calming Pillar. Every time it is used in combat, the dragon veins of the Eastern Sea ripple. Not from anger. From structural damage. The runes along the rod were designed to press down, not to strike. They do not know how to stop pressing even when the rod is raised against heaven's armies. The rod's combat career is the original debt being collected, over and over, on the geography of an entire sea. So let me introduce you to the real cost of that golden glow.
guide.guide_3: Here is where it gets properly terrifying. The material that makes up the rod is called Nine-Turn Smelted Fine Iron. It was forged in Lord Lao Zi's Tushita Palace, which is basically the celestial foundry of the highest Daoist divinity. To smelt this iron, Lao Zi used Samadhi True Fire—a flame so hot that it does not just melt metal; it melts the *laws of reality* embedded in that metal. The rod required a hundred years' worth of intense burning, during which the celestial furnace dimmed. That is not an exaggeration; that is a direct cost from the mythic text. Then the rod was handed to Yu the Great, the flood-tamer who is arguably the most important engineer in Chinese myth. Yu used it to measure and stabilize the floodwaters of the primordial deluge. And after that work was done, what do you do with a giant anchor-law-pillar? You cannot just leave it lying around. So Yu planted it into the deepest abyss of the Eastern Sea, where it extracted the entire stabilizing law of the ocean's water veins. I want you to catch the weight of that. The rod's power to suppress water does not come from a spell cast on it. It comes from a *theft*. The rod permanently removed the Eastern Sea's own ability to self-stabilize, absorbed that principle into its own iron matrix, and left the sea forever dependent on dragon-essence infusions to keep the abyssal eye from collapsing. You are holding a wound. A legalized, permanent theft of the ocean's own equilibrium.
guide.guide_4: Now, here is the part that surprises people: the rod does not actually have a Qi Ling, an artifact spirit. There is no screaming soul trapped inside it, no ancient general's ghost hammering against the iron from within, no sacrificed maiden haunting its rune arrays. This is a departure from many of the artifacts we have discussed tonight. The rod is not an animated prison; it is a preserved law. What gives the rod its responsiveness is the residual lawful imprint of the Eastern Sea's tidal-calming principle—a kind of structural memory that does not think but does *react*. When Sun Wukong says "big," the rod's internal law remembers: this is the direction of expansion. When he says "long," it remembers: this is the direction of reach. But when the rod is activated against a water-controlling enemy, it does not merely strike them. It *suppresses* them. Because deep inside that iron matrix, the law remains convinced that it is still pressing down on the abyssal eye. Anything aquatic that comes within its resonance field is treated as a part of the sea that must be flattened. It is not aggression. It is an automatic response from a law that cannot tell the difference between the ocean and a demon's water magic. That is both better and worse than a screaming ghost. A ghost, at least, you could negotiate with. A law is just going to keep pressing.
guide.guide_5: The rod's relationship with Sun Wukong is the most famous master-artifact bond in Chinese mythology, and it is worth understanding how it actually works. It is not a blood pact. Wukong did not cut his palm, did not recite a binding incantation, did not trade a piece of his soul or a slice of his life span. He walked into the dragon palace, approached the pillar, and the pillar recognized him. The mechanism appears to be a combination of cultivation depth, physical constitution, and what the tradition vaguely calls "destined affinity." The rod's recognition condition seems to be: be strong enough to lift it, and be the one it has been waiting for. Once recognized, the rod accepts the holder's command without any ongoing cost in blood, essence, or life force. This makes the rod relatively benign by artifact standards. There is no Shi Zhu clause hidden in the runes. But—and this is a very important but—that benignity is entirely dependent on *being recognized*. If you try to lift the rod without its recognition, the rod does not just sit there heavy. It actively resists. And its resistance is not a simple rejection; it is a lawful reflection of your own exerted force back into your own body. The dragon princes of the Eastern Sea learned this the hard way. The youngest prince, Ao Bing, attempted to lift the rod before Wukong's arrival—and was found with shattered meridians, a broken body, and a rod that had not even moved an inch. The rod did not attack him. It simply refused to be disrespected. That is a different kind of danger from outright hostility. It is the danger of a tool that obeys only the one who is meant to hold it and punishes everyone else by letting them break themselves against its inertia.
guide.guide_6: Let me tell you about the two people who have held this rod, because the list is very short and very telling. The first was Yu the Great. Yu was a sage-king, a hydraulic engineer of such impossible caliber that he spent thirteen years dredging the flood out of the world, and during his work he held the rod as a measuring tool and an anchor. He did not fight with it. He surveyed the world with it. Then he planted it in the Eastern Sea and left. Yu's own fate, the tradition tells us, was that he ascended to become one of the Five Emperors, a celestial administrator. The rod did not kill him. It did not follow him. It stayed in the abyss and waited. The second—and only—holder is Sun Wukong. The Monkey King claimed the rod during his early career, used it to arm his monkey army, then carried it through his rebellion against Heaven, through his five centuries of imprisonment under Mount Five Elements, and through the Journey to the West. The rod has never betrayed him. It has never attacked him. It has, within the limits of a law-holding iron pillar, been loyal. But notice something: Wukong is not a typical cultivator. He is a being of immense native power, born from primordial stone, trained under immortal masters, armed with the Eight-Nine Mystical Arts, and carrying a nature that is half-spirit-trickster and half-god-rebel. He is the exact kind of being that the rod's recognition mechanism was designed for—someone strong enough to command its full expression without needing to drain its reserves. If you or I tried to wield the rod, we would be broken before we could lift it an inch. The rod's loyalty is not an invitation. It is a filter.
guide.guide_7: So let me leave you with this thought. The As-You-Will Golden-Banded Rod is arguably the most famous weapon in Chinese myth. It is also one of the least bloody in its own cost structure. There is no imprisoned soul inside it, no body count from blood sacrifice, no active draining of its master's life force. But it still carries a cosmic theft in its bones—the stolen stability of an entire sea. Every time Sun Wukong swings that rod, the Eastern Sea's dragon veins shudder. The abyssal eye that the rod was designed to seal has been left as an open wound that requires constant expenditure from the dragon clan to keep from collapsing entirely. The rod is not a happy tool. It is a law that was extracted from a living geography and left a permanent scar in exchange for its power. The Monkey King is not a tyrant for using it—he did not cause the theft, and he cannot undo it. But the weight of that original debt is real, and it is still being paid. Every time the rod expands, the earth beneath the sea contracts a little more. That is the quiet truth behind the golden glow and the world-echoing thunder. This is the fundamental logic of this universe: power is never free. If it is not your own blood, it is someone else's geography. Or someone else's law. Or someone else's sea. The rod remembers its theft, and the Eastern Sea has not yet finished paying for it. That, to me, is the most honest thing about this weapon. It does not pretend to be clean.

seo.meta_description: An encyclopedia entry on the As-You-Will Golden-Banded Rod (如意金箍棒), the legendary divine pillar and weapon of Sun Wukong. This entry covers the rod's origin from Lord Lao Zi's furnace, its extraction of the Eastern Sea's stabilizing law, its 'As-You-Will' principle, its recognition ritual, and the accumulated structural damage to the Eastern Sea caused by every activation of its tidal-calming runes.
seo.og_title: As-You-Will Golden-Banded Rod (如意金箍棒) — The Pillar That Stole an Ocean's Law | Eastern Mythology Encyclopedia

The As-You-Will Golden-Banded Rod was forged from Nine-Turn Smelted Iron, originally planted as a law-anchor in the Eastern Sea. Beneath its combat power lies a permanent theft—the ocean's own stability, extracted and sealed within iron.

lore_entries.surface_form: Nine-Turn Smelted Fine Iron (九转镔铁)
lore_entries.description: The celestial iron alloy from which the rod was forged, refined through nine cycles of Samadhi True Fire in Lord Lao Zi's furnace and dimming the flame for a century.
A Strange Fire capable of melting not only metal but the structural laws of reality; used in Lord Lao Zi's palace for forging divine treasures.
The celestial foundry and palace of Lord Lao Zi in Daoist cosmology, where high-level artifacts are refined.
The deepest point of a sea's stabilizing nexus; the Eastern Sea's abyssal eye was permanently damaged when the rod extracted its tidal law.

lore_entries.surface_form: One hundred thirty thousand five hundred jin (一万三千五百斤)
lore_entries.description: The fixed baseline mass of the rod in mythic tradition; a weight that only a recognized master can bear.

lore_entries.surface_form: Eastern Sea Dragon Clan (东海龙族)
lore_entries.description: The clan of dragon-divinities who govern the Eastern Sea and bear the ongoing cost of sustaining its abyssal eye after the rod's removal.

faq_entries.question: Did the rod kill its original owner, Yu the Great?
faq_entries.answer: No. Yu the Great used the rod as a surveying tool and anchor during the flood-quelling era, then left it in the Eastern Sea. He ascended to become one of the Five Emperors without any record of harm from the rod.

faq_entries.question: Does the rod drain Sun Wukong's life force when he uses it?
faq_entries.answer: No. The rod does not drain the holder during normal use. Its recognition mechanism is based on cultivation depth, not ongoing blood tribute. The accumulated cost is paid by the Eastern Sea's dragon veins, not the wielder's vitality.

faq_entries.question: Is there a soul trapped inside the rod?
faq_entries.answer: No. The rod contains no Qi Ling (artifact spirit) in the form of a sealed soul. Its responsiveness comes from the residual lawful imprint of the tidal-calming principle extracted from the Eastern Sea's abyssal eye, and from the innate "As-You-Will" property imparted by Lord Lao Zi's forging.

faq_entries.question: Why can't other beings lift the rod?
faq_entries.answer: The rod's recognition mechanism requires sufficient cultivation depth and physical constitution to bear its baseline mass, combined with a quality of spiritual affinity that the tradition calls "destined fate." Unrecognized beings who attempt to lift it suffer crushing internal injuries as the rod's lawful inertia reflects their own exerted power back through their meridians.

faq_entries.question: What happens if the rod's tidal-calming runes are activated too many times?
faq_entries.answer: Each activation sends a shockwave through the Eastern Sea's dragon veins, causing incremental structural damage. The tradition records that accumulated activations have caused partial collapses of certain deep-sea trenches in the Eastern Sea's abyssal ecosystem. No precise threshold or catastrophic endpoint is given.
